chapter: Reel 3: defining jazz and the blues
title: Sonny Greer, Bubber Miley and Nat King Cole
summary: Short remarks on Sonny Greer, trumpeter Bubber Miley's plunger style, and Nat King Cole as an acquaintance.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Growl, plunger and derby: the trumpet mute tradition

blocks.x: Did you know Sonny Greer?
Yes, he was a drummer with Duke Ellington for many years. Started with Duke Ellington.
Uh huh. You know, he's 82 now.
He is?
And he's playing in New York.
Yeah?
And I thought maybe some day we might be able to ...
Where is he playing in New York?
The West End Club, or something like that.
Oh yes -- that's right.
Do you know where that is?
No, I don't know where it is, but I did see it in one of the writeups.
Right, right.
Yes.
In one of the little things I read about him, he told how a trumpet player, Bubber Miley? Does that ring a bell with you?
Yes, Bubber Miley, yes, he was a trumpet player.
And he used a plunger at the end of his trumpet to get some fantastic sounds.
Yes, he did.
That's like the ultimate in improvisational techniques in music.
Yes, he did; he had a style of his own -- Bubber Miley.
So we've got the J.C. Johnson definition of blues in your poem.
Yes.
Okay. What can you tell us about, say, Nat King Cole?
Nat King Cole? I can't tell you too much about him. I knew him, but we weren't what you might call intimate friends. We were friends, but not intimate friends.
Well ... (CUT)
